st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: Johnson v. Dunn accepts continuing human accountability and materially develops the cluster by extending verification responsibility to every signing or filing attorney, even those unaware of AI use, while distinguishing individual misconduct from firm culpability. It also grounds sanctions in inherent authority because Rule 11 did not govern the discovery motions, reinforcing that consequences depend on authority, culpability and procedural context.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts the cluster’s human-led, verification-dependent model and materially develops it through a concrete sanctions case. It shows that nominal lawyer involvement is insufficient: responsibility remains personal at filing, while safe deployment requires citation-level verification, clear signatory duties, training and prefiling controls.

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Johnson supports the proposition that AI use does not displace lawyers’ personal, nondelegable duties of reasonable inquiry and citation accuracy. It also aligns with the cluster’s procedural qualifications by holding that Rule 11 did not govern the discovery motions while treating its deterrence rationale as persuasive and recognizing other, separately constrained sanctions or disciplinary mechanisms.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: Johnson v. Dunn strongly supports the cluster’s central proposition. It holds lawyers and supervisors accountable for unchecked fabricated citations regardless of who used AI, treats even cursory verification as required, and bases sanctions on reckless or bad-faith inquiry failures rather than AI use itself. Its reliance on inherent authority where specific rules did not clearly apply also fits the cluster’s technology-neutral governance framing.

kp.k: Unverified ChatGPT research produced false statements of law
kp.d: In its July 23, 2025 opinion, the court found five problematic citations across two discovery motions filed in May 2025. Matthew B. Reeves admitted using ChatGPT to obtain supporting authorities without independently verifying them. The citations included nonexistent cases and combinations of case names, citations and propositions that did not correspond to genuine authority. The court treated these as false statements of law, not merely unsuccessful legal arguments.

kp.k: Rule gaps required reliance on inherent sanctioning authority
kp.d: The court held that Rule 11 did not apply because the filings were discovery motions under Rules 30 and 37, while finding those discovery rules supplied no basis for addressing these false statements of law. It declined to extend Alabama Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3 beyond knowing misstatements, given the absence of verification and two lawyers' lack of knowledge that AI had been used. Local Rule 83.1(f) did not clearly resolve the gap. The court therefore used its inherent authority, requiring subjective bad faith or conduct tantamount to it rather than simple recklessness.

kp.k: Reliance on supervisors did not excuse missing verification
kp.d: William J. Cranford drafted, signed and filed both motions, incorporating Reeves's authorities while checking grammar and typography rather than the authorities themselves. Although he did not know ChatGPT had been used, the court found his repeated failure to check citations particularly egregious and tantamount to bad faith. The opinion distinguishes such complete failures of verification from occasional typographical errors or reasonable disagreements over legal authority.

kp.k: Supervisory accountability extended beyond personally using AI
kp.d: The court also found William R. Lunsford's conduct tantamount to bad faith. As practice group leader, supervisory partner and designated deputy attorney general, he allowed his name to appear on the motions without verifying the authorities or requiring another person to do so. The court criticised a workflow based on assuming others checked citations and reusing material from earlier filings. His immediate effort to avoid the show cause hearing compounded its concerns. These were individual findings, not a rule imposing sanctions merely because a name appeared on a filing.

kp.k: Firm safeguards supported release without institutional sanctions
kp.d: The court separately assessed Butler Snow's own conduct and found no evidentiary basis for bad faith or equivalent recklessness. The firm had warned attorneys about inaccurate AI output in June 2023, required permission for using new technology as a secondary research tool with traditional accuracy checks, and required verification of CoCounsel outputs when introducing that product in January 2025. Its warnings, investigation and remedial response supported release without sanction. Chism and Potter were also released based on their lack of relevant involvement; Dunn was not sanctioned because he was unaware of the conduct.

kp.k: Remediation required extensive human review and stronger protocols
kp.d: Butler Snow reported reviewing 52 Alabama federal court dockets, of which 40 contained substantive citations, covering relevant filings on or after April 1, 2023. A separate Morgan Lewis team of twenty-eight attorneys verified citations in those same 40 dockets, reviewing more than 2,400 separate legal citations across 330 filings. Its declaration reported no additional fabricated citations or citations to legitimate sources that did not support the stated proposition. Butler Snow also committed to additional training and a prefiling protocol checking each authority's existence, accuracy and relevance. The firm said the State of Alabama would bear none of the associated costs.

kp.k: False authorities harm proceedings despite correct legal propositions
kp.d: The court described wasted opposing-party resources, judicial investigation and hearings, case delay and potential damage to public confidence. Drawing partly on Mata v. Avianca, it also identified reputational and systemic harms. It rejected mitigation based on genuine authorities supporting the same legal propositions, reasoning that this did not undo the harm and would encourage unverified AI use. Its warning of escalating costs and disruption if misuse continued was a prospective judicial assessment, not a quantified empirical finding.

kp.k: Court imposed professional consequences beyond modest monetary sanctions
kp.d: The court considered fines and ordinary public embarrassment insufficient deterrents in this case, citing the continuing appearance of AI-citation sanctions incidents. It publicly reprimanded Reeves, Cranford and Lunsford, disqualified them from this case and referred the matter to applicable licensing authorities. They had to distribute the order within ten days to clients, opposing counsel and presiding judges in every pending case in which they were counsel of record, and to every attorney in their firm. The court declined district-wide suspension because the investigations, remorse and Reeves's educational commitment supported a narrower sanction. Its conclusion about deterrence was judicial reasoning, not a measured comparison of sanction effectiveness.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Anna M. Manasco presents unverified AI-generated legal citations as a source of litigation harm requiring human verification and stronger professional accountability.
pts.d: In this July 2025 sanctions opinion, Manasco finds that ChatGPT-generated citations introduced into two discovery motions were false statements of law. She argues that such misuse wastes opposing parties' resources, diverts judicial attention, delays substantive proceedings, and can undermine public confidence. She predicts escalating costs and disruption unless misuse is promptly checked. She considers fines and public embarrassment insufficient deterrents in this case and imposes public reprimands with publication requirements, disqualification from the case, and referrals to licensing authorities. Responsibility extends beyond the lawyer who used ChatGPT: the filing lawyer and a supervisory partner were also sanctioned for verification failures despite not knowing that AI had generated the citations. Separately, Butler Snow general counsel Benjamin Watson describes institutional changes prompted by the incident, including additional training and a prefiling citation-verification protocol. These are claims about professional duties, litigation processes, and institutional responses, not predictions of lawyer displacement or market-wide productivity gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on the case record, attorney admissions, firm policies, retrospective citation reviews, and other sanctions decisions rather than model-performance benchmarks.
pts.d: The court identified five problematic citations across two motions filed in May 2025, conducted independent searches, and considered written declarations and testimony at a May 21 show cause hearing. Reeves admitted using ChatGPT and failing to verify its citations; Cranford described checking supervisors' edits for grammar and typography but not independently reviewing the added legal authorities. The record also documents warnings and policies predating the incident. Butler Snow reviewed 52 Alabama federal court dockets, 40 of which contained substantive citations, and commissioned Morgan Lewis to independently check more than 2,400 citations across 330 filings. Morgan Lewis partner Scott Milner reported no additional fabricated citations or citations to legitimate sources that failed to support the proposition offered. That bounded retrospective review helped support the court's decision against district-wide suspension; it is not a measured hallucination rate for ChatGPT or legal-AI systems generally. Manasco's deterrence argument draws on repeated sanctions incidents, including Mata and subsequent cases, and her assessment of their consequences, not a controlled study of sanction effectiveness.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The opinion addresses misconduct in May 2025, calls for immediate deterrence, and conditions sanctions on individualized responsibility and particularly egregious verification failures.
pts.d: The order was signed July 23, 2025. Its future-harm prediction is conditional on unchecked continuation of AI misuse and supplies no numerical forecast or fixed prediction horizon. The relevant firm safeguards began with a June 2023 warning and approval policy; a January 2025 CoCounsel policy required verification before reliance. Watson's additional training and prefiling protocol were prospective commitments. The court does not prohibit AI use as such or equate all errors with sanctionable bad faith: it distinguishes fabricated authorities from minor typographical mistakes and reasonably debatable legal positions. Rule 11 did not apply because the filings were discovery motions under Rules 30 and 37. The court also declined to extend Alabama Rule of Professional Conduct 3.3 beyond its knowing-misstatement language without state-court guidance, instead relying on inherent authority and findings of recklessness tantamount to bad faith. Prior warnings, repeated failures to check, and individual roles were central. The firm's reasonable prevention and remediation efforts, the independent review, and the lawyers' remorse limited the sanctions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The effects encompass litigation teams, their firms and clients, opposing parties, courts, and the public, with responsibility differentiated by participation and supervisory role.
pts.d: Reeves, a partner and assistant practice group leader, was sanctioned for inserting unverified ChatGPT citations; Cranford, of counsel, for signing and filing without checking them; and Lunsford, the practice group leader and designated deputy attorney general, for his egregious supervisory and verification failures concerning filings bearing his name. Each was disqualified from this case and required to distribute the order to clients, opposing counsel, and judges in pending cases, as well as every attorney at the firm. Associate Daniel Chism and attorney Lynette Potter were released without sanction on the uncontested evidence of their nonparticipation and the other role-specific circumstances. Butler Snow was not sanctioned but undertook internal and external reviews and committed to stronger safeguards, at its own expense rather than the State's. Defendant Dunn was not sanctioned because he lacked prior awareness; replacement counsel were allowed thirty days to prepare. The court identifies the incarcerated plaintiff and opposing counsel as bearing the burden of uncovering fabrication, courts as bearing investigation and delay costs, and the public as facing potential loss of confidence. The case illustrates that experienced lawyers at a large firm with established research resources are not insulated from AI-related verification failures.
